title: A welcome sign for the screen
brief: Hi! I run the Cafe du Port. I just put a little screen above the counter. Can your machine show our welcome message on it? Three lines, exactly as I wrote them below.

skill.title: print() puts text on the screen
skill.card: Every program talks through print(). Put text between quotes inside the brackets and it appears on the screen, one line per call.

task:
Print these three lines, in this order, exactly:

~~~text
Welcome to Cafe du Port
Today: lemon tart
Open until 19:00
~~~
solution:
print("Welcome to Cafe du Port")
print("Today: lemon tart")
print("Open until 19:00")
hint: One print() per line. Copy each sentence between double quotes.

tests.output:
Welcome to Cafe du Port
Today: lemon tart
Open until 19:00

title: Split the bill
brief: Tables of friends always ask to split the bill. My waiters lose minutes with a calculator. The total and the number of people are already in the code. Print what each person pays, rounded to 2 decimals.

skill.title: Variables and arithmetic
skill.card: A variable is a name that holds a value: total = 87.5. Python does maths with + - * /, and round(x, 2) keeps 2 decimals.

task: Using the variables total and people, print one line: Each pays: followed by total / people rounded to 2 decimals. Do not type the numbers yourself: the client will change them.
starter:
total = 87.5
people = 3
# print what each person pays
solution:
total = 87.5
people = 3
print("Each pays:", round(total / people, 2))
hint: print("Each pays:", round(total / people, 2)) prints the label and the number with a space between them.
test: assert 'total' in dir() and 'people' in dir(), 'Keep the variables total and people.'

title: Add the tip
brief: Your splitter is a hit! One change: we now add a 10 percent tip before splitting. And show the tip on its own line first, please.
task: Print two lines: ~~~text Tip: 8.75 Each pays: 32.08 ~~~ The tip is 10 percent of total. Each person pays (total + tip) / people, rounded to 2 decimals.
solution:
total = 87.5
people = 3
tip = total * 0.10
print("Tip:", round(tip, 2))
print("Each pays:", round((total + tip) / people, 2))
hint: Compute tip = total * 0.10 first, then reuse it in the second print.

title: Tidy the job ticket
brief: Customers fill in the drop off card any way they like: capitals everywhere, spaces before and after. My workshop screen needs it tidy. Can your machine clean the name and the plate before they go on the job ticket?

skill.title: String methods and f-strings
skill.card: strip() removes the outer spaces, title() capitalises each word and upper() capitalises everything. split() cuts on spaces and "-".join(parts) glues the pieces back with a separator. An f-string drops values into text: f"{a} | {b}".
skill.example:
name = "  paul MARTIN "
print(name.strip().title())
print("-".join("ab 12 cd".upper().split()))
word = "Garage"
print(word[0], word[-1], word[0:3])

task: Starting from name and plate, build three variables: - clean: the name without outer spaces, each word capitalised (Sophie Bernard) - plate_id: the plate in capitals, pieces joined with - (EF-482-GH) - initials: the first letter of each of the two words of clean (SB) Then print the ticket line with an f-string: ~~~text Sophie Bernard | EF-482-GH | SB ~~~
starter:
name = "  sophie BERNARD  "
plate = "ef 482 gh"
# build clean, plate_id and initials, then print the ticket line
solution:
name = "  sophie BERNARD  "
plate = "ef 482 gh"
clean = name.strip().title()
plate_id = "-".join(plate.upper().split())
words = clean.split()
initials = words[0][0] + words[1][0]
print(f"{clean} | {plate_id} | {initials}")
hint: clean = name.strip().title(). For the plate: plate.upper().split() gives the pieces, "-".join(...) glues them.
test:
assert clean == 'Sophie Bernard', 'clean should be Sophie Bernard, got %r' % (clean,)
assert plate_id == 'EF-482-GH', 'plate_id should be EF-482-GH, got %r' % (plate_id,)
assert initials == 'SB', 'initials should be SB, got %r' % (initials,)

title: Price the stay
brief: At check out, reception types the number of nights and the nightly rate, then works out the bill on paper. We get it wrong every week. Your machine reads both numbers and prints the stay total.

skill.title: input() reads text, int() and float() turn it into numbers
skill.card: input() reads one typed line and always gives back a string. int() turns it into a whole number, float() into a decimal. Convert before doing maths: "3" * "2" is an error.
skill.example:
nights = int("3")
rate = float("89.5")
print(f"{nights} nights: {nights * rate}")

task:
Read two lines: the number of nights (whole number), then the nightly rate (decimal). Print one line, the total rounded to 2 decimals:

~~~text
3 nights x 89.5 = 268.5
~~~
starter:
nights = input()
rate = input()
print(f"{nights} nights x {rate} = {nights * rate}")
solution:
nights = int(input())
rate = float(input())
print(f"{nights} nights x {rate} = {round(nights * rate, 2)}")
hint: nights = int(input()) and rate = float(input()). Then round(nights * rate, 2) inside the f-string.

task: Read two lines: the customer name, then the plate. Clean them exactly as before and print the same ticket line. For input jean-luc roche and ab 12 cd: ~~~text Jean-Luc Roche | AB-12-CD | JR ~~~

name = input()

clean = name.strip().title()
plate_id = "-".join(plate.upper().split())
words = clean.split()

title: Delivery fee rules
brief: We deliver groceries in town. Orders of 50 euros or more travel free, from 20 up to 50 it costs 4.90, and under 20 we charge 7.90. My staff keep mixing up the rules, so let the machine decide.

skill.title: if, elif, else
skill.card: if runs its indented block only when the condition is true. Python checks if then each elif in order and runs the first that matches; else catches the rest. So test the highest threshold first.

task: Read the order amount (decimal). Print the delivery line, then the amount to pay rounded to 2 decimals: - 50 or more: Delivery: free, fee 0 - 20 or more: Delivery: 4.9 - below 20: Delivery: 7.9 For 35: ~~~text Delivery: 4.9 To pay: 39.9 ~~~
starter:
amount = float(input())
# choose the fee, then print the two lines
solution:
amount = float(input())
if amount >= 50:
    fee = 0
    print("Delivery: free")
elif amount >= 20:
    fee = 4.9
    print("Delivery: 4.9")
else:
    fee = 7.9
    print("Delivery: 7.9")
print(f"To pay: {round(amount + fee, 2)}")
hint: Start with if amount >= 50, then elif amount >= 20, then else. Set fee in each branch and print To pay once at the end.

title: A backup till
brief: The till broke again and the repair man comes on Monday. Until then my staff type how many items are on the tray, then each price. Number each line on the receipt and give me the total at the bottom.

skill.title: for and range()
skill.card: A for loop repeats its block once per item. range(1, n + 1) counts 1, 2, ..., n because the stop value is never included. To add things up, start a variable at 0 before the loop and add to it inside.
skill.example:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 4):
    print(f"Line {i}")
    total = total + i
print(total)

task: Read n, then n prices (decimals), one per line. Print each price with its line number, then the total rounded to 2 decimals. For 3 items: ~~~text 1: 2.5 2: 1.8 3: 3.0 Total: 7.3 ~~~
starter:
n = int(input())
total = 0
# read each price, print it, add it to total
print(f"Total: {total}")
solution:
n = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    price = float(input())
    print(f"{i}: {price}")
    total = total + price
print(f"Total: {round(total, 2)}")
hint: for i in range(1, n + 1): read the price with float(input()) inside the loop, print it, then total = total + price.

task: Right now an order of exactly 50 pays 4.9 delivery and an order of exactly 20 pays 7.9. The rules are still: 50 or more is free, 20 or more pays 4.9, below 20 pays 7.9. Make every test pass.

if amount > 50:

elif amount > 20:
    fee = 4.9
    print("Delivery: 4.9")
else:
    fee = 7.9
    print("Delivery: 7.9")
print(f"To pay: {round(amount + fee, 2)}")
solution:
amount = float(input())
if amount >= 50:
    fee = 0
    print("Delivery: free")
elif amount >= 20:

    print("Delivery: 4.9")

title: Coach timesheets
brief: My coaches send their week one line per day: the hours they worked, or off. They finish with done. Payroll needs the number of days worked and the total hours, and I am tired of counting by hand.

skill.title: while True, break and continue
skill.card: When you do not know how many lines will come, loop with while True: and leave with break when you see the end marker. continue skips the rest of this round and goes straight to the next one. days += 1 is short for days = days + 1.
skill.example:
lines = ["4", "off", "6", "done"]
i = 0
total = 0
while True:
    line = lines[i]
    i += 1
    if line == "done":
        break
    if line == "off":
        continue
    total += int(line)
print(total)

task: Read lines until the line done. Skip the lines off. Every other line is a whole number of hours for one day worked. Print: ~~~text Days worked: 3 Hours: 22 ~~~
starter:
days = 0
hours = 0
# read lines until done
print(f"Days worked: {days}")
print(f"Hours: {hours}")
solution:
days = 0
hours = 0
while True:
    line = input()
    if line == "done":
        break
    if line == "off":
        continue
    days += 1
    hours += int(line)
print(f"Days worked: {days}")
print(f"Hours: {hours}")
hint: Inside while True: read line = input(). If it is done, break. If it is off, continue. Otherwise add 1 to days and int(line) to hours.

title: Loyalty discount on the till
brief: Regulars love the new receipts. We are starting a loyalty deal: when a tray reaches 20 euros, take 10 percent off. Show the discount on its own line so they see it.
task: After the numbered lines, if the total is 20 or more, print Discount: with 10 percent of the total rounded to 2 decimals, and take it off the total. The last line is still Total: rounded to 2 decimals. Below 20, nothing changes. For a 22 euro tray: ~~~text 1: 8.5 2: 6.0 3: 4.5 4: 3.0 Discount: 2.2 Total: 19.8 ~~~
solution:
n = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    price = float(input())
    print(f"{i}: {price}")
    total = total + price
if total >= 20:
    discount = round(total * 0.1, 2)
    print(f"Discount: {discount}")
    total = total - discount
print(f"Total: {round(total, 2)}")
hint: After the loop: if total >= 20, compute the discount, print it, then subtract it from total.

title: End of day sales
brief: Every evening I type the day's sales into the machine. I want to see how many we made, the best one, the average, and the big tickets above 100 euros so I can send those customers a thank you card.

skill.title: Lists: append, len, sum, max
skill.card: A list keeps values in order: start empty with sales = [] and add with sales.append(x). len(), sum(), max() and min() work on the whole list. To keep only some values, loop and append the ones you want to a second list.
skill.example:
sales = []
sales.append(45.0)
sales.append(120.0)
print(len(sales), sum(sales), max(sales))
big = []
for s in sales:
    if s > 100:
        big.append(s)
print(big)

task: Read n, then n sale amounts (decimals) into a list sales. Build big: the sales strictly above 100, in the same order. Print (average rounded to 1 decimal): ~~~text Sales: 5 Best: 420.0 Average: 151.2 Big: [420.0, 180.0] ~~~
starter:
n = int(input())
sales = []
# fill sales, build big, print the four lines
solution:
n = int(input())
sales = []
for i in range(n):
    sales.append(float(input()))
big = []
for s in sales:
    if s > 100:
        big.append(s)
print(f"Sales: {len(sales)}")
print(f"Best: {max(sales)}")
print(f"Average: {round(sum(sales) / len(sales), 1)}")
print(f"Big: {big}")
hint: Average: round(sum(sales) / len(sales), 1). Printing a list inside an f-string shows it with its brackets.
test: assert isinstance(sales, list) and isinstance(big, list), 'Keep the lists sales and big.'

title: Parts used today
brief: After each job the mechanic types the part and how many he used. At closing I want one count per part so I know what to reorder, and the part we burn through fastest.

skill.title: Dictionaries count things
skill.card: A dict maps keys to values: used["filter"] = 3. used.get(key, 0) gives 0 when the key is not there yet, which is perfect for adding up. for key, value in used.items() walks the pairs in the order they were added, and max(used, key=used.get) gives the key with the biggest value.

task: Read n, then n lines part qty (for example filter 2). Add the quantities per part in a dict used. Print one line per part in the order they first appear, then the part with the biggest total: ~~~text filter: 3 brake_pad: 5 wiper: 2 Top: brake_pad ~~~
hint: words = input().split() gives ["filter", "2"]. Then used[words[0]] = used.get(words[0], 0) + int(words[1]).
test: assert isinstance(used, dict), 'Keep the dict used.'

task: Days marked off are counted in Days worked. They must not be. Hours are fine. Make every test pass.

    days += 1

        continue
    hours += int(line)
print(f"Days worked: {days}")
print(f"Hours: {hours}")
solution:
days = 0
hours = 0
while True:

    if line == "off":

title: Catch double bookings
brief: We sell rooms on two booking sites and sometimes both sell the same room for tonight. Each site sends me one line of room numbers. Show me the clashes so I can call the guests, and how many rooms are taken in total.

skill.title: Sets: unique values, & and |
skill.card: set(...) keeps each value once. a & b keeps what is in both sets, a | b everything in either. A set has no order: sorted() turns it into a sorted list.
skill.example:
a = set("101 104 104".split())
b = {"104", "202"}
print(sorted(a & b))
print(len(a | b))

task: Read two lines of room numbers separated by spaces (a line can repeat a room). Build the sets site_a and site_b. Print the rooms in both, sorted and separated by spaces, or none, then the number of distinct rooms booked: ~~~text Clashes: 104 210 Rooms taken: 5 ~~~
starter:
site_a = input()
site_b = input()
# find the clashes and count the rooms
solution:
site_a = set(input().split())
site_b = set(input().split())
clashes = sorted(site_a & site_b)
if len(clashes) > 0:
    print("Clashes: " + " ".join(clashes))
else:
    print("Clashes: none")
print(f"Rooms taken: {len(site_a | site_b)}")
hint: set(input().split()) builds each set. " ".join(sorted(site_a & site_b)) gives the clash line.
test: assert isinstance(site_a, set) and isinstance(site_b, set), 'site_a and site_b should be sets.'

title: Weekend promo prices
brief: Weekend promo: everything is 20 percent off. My supplier sends the price list as one line of name:price. I need the new prices for the shelf labels, and the bargain list: what costs under 2 euros after the promo.

skill.title: Comprehensions
skill.card: A comprehension builds a list or a dict in one line: [x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0] or {k: v for ...}. Read it as: this value, for each item, if the condition holds.

task: Read one line such as apples:2.40 milk:1.10 coffee:6.50. With comprehensions, build the dict promo (name to price times 0.8, rounded to 2 decimals) and the list bargains (names whose promo price is below 2, in the same order). Print one line per product, then the bargains joined by , : ~~~text apples: 1.92 milk: 0.88 coffee: 5.2 Bargains: apples, milk ~~~
starter:
items = input().split()
# build promo and bargains with comprehensions
hint: For one item like "milk:1.10", i.split(":")[0] is the name and i.split(":")[1] the price text.

tests.name: Fruit and drinks
tests.output:
apples: 1.92
milk: 0.88
coffee: 5.2
Bargains: apples, milk

test: assert isinstance(promo, dict) and isinstance(bargains, list), 'Build the dict promo and the list bargains.'

title: Reorder flags
brief: The parts count saves me an hour a week. My supplier wants the list in alphabetical order, and mark anything we used 3 or more of so I remember to reorder it.
task: Print the parts sorted by name. Add REORDER at the end of the line when the total is 3 or more. The Top line stays as it is: ~~~text brake_pad: 5 REORDER filter: 3 REORDER wiper: 2 Top: brake_pad ~~~
hint: for part in sorted(used): gives the keys in alphabetical order. used[part] is the total.

wiper: 2

title: One price for every quote
brief: Three people answer the phone at my guesthouse and they all count differently. I want one function everyone uses: nights, nightly rate, breakfast or not. Breakfast is 12 euros per night.

skill.title: Functions with return and default values
skill.card: def name(a, b=False): packages code you can call again. return hands a value back to the caller; printing is not returning. A parameter with = has a default value, used when the caller leaves it out.
skill.example:
def price(nights, rate, breakfast=False):
    total = nights * rate
    if breakfast:
        total = total + 12 * nights
    return total
print(price(2, 50))
print(price(2, 50, True))

task: Write stay_price(nights, rate, breakfast=False): nights times rate, plus 12 per night when breakfast is true, rounded to 2 decimals. Write quote_line(name, total) returning Quote for Martin: 306.0. Then read four lines (name, nights, rate, yes or no for breakfast) and print the quote line.
starter:
def stay_price(nights, rate, breakfast=False):
    pass

def quote_line(name, total):
    pass

name = input()
nights = int(input())
rate = float(input())
breakfast = input() == "yes"
print(quote_line(name, stay_price(nights, rate, breakfast)))
hint: Inside stay_price, compute total, add 12 * nights if breakfast, then return round(total, 2).
test:
assert stay_price(2, 50) == 100, 'stay_price(2, 50) should return 100'
assert stay_price(2, 50, True) == 124, 'stay_price(2, 50, True) should return 124'
assert stay_price(1, 80, breakfast=True) == 92, 'stay_price(1, 80, breakfast=True) should return 92'
assert quote_line('Ana', 10.5) == 'Quote for Ana: 10.5', 'quote_line should return the text, not print it'

title: Rowing challenge board
brief: This month we run a 500 metre rowing challenge. Times come in as name and seconds. I want the board on the big screen, fastest first, with the club average under it.

skill.title: *args and lambda sort keys
skill.card: def average(*times): accepts any number of arguments and receives them as a tuple. A star in a call spreads a list into arguments: average(*laps). sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1]) sorts rows by their second value.

task: Write average(*times) returning the average of its arguments rounded to 1 decimal. Read n, then n lines name seconds into a list results of tuples (name, seconds). Sort them fastest first with a lambda into board, print the ranking, then the average: ~~~text 1. Ami 95 2. Zoe 98 3. Tom 105 4. Luc 112 Average: 102.5 ~~~
starter:
def average(*times):
    pass

n = int(input())
results = []
# read the times, sort them, print the board
hint: board = sorted(results, key=lambda r: r[1]). For the average, build the list of seconds with a comprehension and spread it with *.
test:
assert average(100, 101) == 100.5 and average(90) == 90, 'average should accept any number of times'
assert board == sorted(results, key=lambda r: r[1]), 'board should be results sorted by seconds'

title: Quote a custom bike
brief: Custom builds are quoted as nested lists: the frame, then the wheel set, which holds the rims, which hold the spokes, and so on. My spreadsheet chokes on it. I need the number of priced parts and the full quote, however deep the nesting goes.

skill.title: Recursion on nested lists
skill.card: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller piece. For nested lists: loop over the items, and when isinstance(item, list) is true, call the same function on that item and use what it returns. A plain value is the base case.

task: Write count(parts) returning how many numbers the nested list holds, and total(parts) returning their sum rounded to 2 decimals. Both must work at any depth. Then print, for build: ~~~text Parts: 8 Quote: 577.3 ~~~
hint: In both functions, if the item is a list, add what the function returns for that item; otherwise add the item (or 1 for count).
test:
assert count([1, [2, [3]]]) == 3 and count([[], [[]]]) == 0, 'count must go into every level'
assert total([1, [2, [3]]]) == 6 and total([]) == 0, 'total must add every level'
assert total([[10.5], [[0.25, [0.25]]]]) == 11, 'total([[10.5], [[0.25, [0.25]]]]) should be 11'
